body_markdown:
Proposed UK cohabitation law changes could give some unmarried partners greater financial rights after separation. Here is what the reforms could mean for property, pensions, savings and family finances.


If you live with a partner but are not married, a proposed change to family law could significantly alter what happens to your finances if the relationship ends.


The UK Government has been consulting on plans to strengthen financial protections for eligible cohabiting couples in England and Wales. Under the proposals, some unmarried partners could potentially ask a court for financial help after a separation if they cannot meet their basic needs.


The proposals are not yet law. The Government's consultation, titled **A Fairer End to Relationships** , closed on 14 August 2026 and is intended to help shape possible future legislation.


So what could the proposed cohabitation law changes mean for your home, savings, pension and other assets?


## Why are cohabitation laws being reviewed?


A common misconception in the UK is that couples who have lived together for years automatically acquire the same financial rights as married couples.


They do not.


In England and Wales, there is no general legal status known as "common law marriage" that automatically gives unmarried partners the financial protections available to spouses.


If a couple separates, the existing legal position can therefore be very different depending on how property is owned, what agreements were made and whether there are children involved.


The Government says the current system can leave cohabitants facing significant financial difficulties after a relationship ends, particularly where one partner has taken time away from paid employment to provide childcare or has become financially dependent on the other partner.


## Who could benefit from the proposed changes?


The proposed framework would apply to qualifying cohabitants rather than every unmarried couple.


The Government has proposed eligibility for adults in committed and interdependent relationships who have lived together for at least three years. Couples who have a child together could qualify after living together for any period.


The proposals are intended to provide additional protection where simply dividing assets according to legal ownership would leave one partner or their children unable to meet their basic needs.


This could be particularly important where one person has sacrificed earnings or career opportunities to care for children.


The Government has also highlighted the financial difficulties faced by survivors of domestic abuse, including economic abuse, when they try to leave a relationship.


## Could your ex really get a share of your assets?


Potentially, but the proposed system would not simply mean that an ex-partner automatically receives half of everything you own.


That distinction is important.


Under the proposals, each partner would generally retain the assets they legally own. However, a court could intervene where the normal ownership position would not provide enough money or resources to meet the basic needs of the partners or their children.


The court could consider factors such as each person's income, earning capacity, financial resources, age, disability and the length of the relationship.


Children's needs would be given particular importance.


The proposals therefore appear to be focused on preventing serious financial hardship rather than creating an automatic 50/50 division of wealth.


## What could a court order?


The proposed legislation could give courts a range of powers similar to some of those available in divorce cases, although the Government intends the cohabitation scheme to be narrower.


Possible remedies include orders affecting property, lump-sum payments and pension sharing.


Ongoing maintenance would be much more restricted and would only be available in exceptional circumstances, such as serious health problems or disability. Any such payment would also be intended to last for a defined and limited period.


Applications would generally need to be made within two years of the relationship ending.


The proposals also favour a "clean break" where possible, meaning financial issues would ideally be resolved without creating long-term financial dependence between former partners.


## How is this different from getting divorced?


Marriage and cohabitation would still have different legal consequences.


The proposed cohabitation framework would not introduce an automatic 50/50 split of assets. It would also take a narrower approach to financial needs than the system used when a marriage ends.


Discretionary spending and luxuries would not generally form part of the assessment of needs.


The Government also proposes that shorter relationships could result in more limited awards, meaning a relationship that only just meets the qualifying period could potentially be treated differently from a much longer partnership.


In other words, owning an expensive house or having substantial savings would not automatically mean an unmarried ex could claim them. The proposed test would focus on whether financial assistance is genuinely required to meet eligible needs.


## Why has the proposal attracted criticism?


Not everyone agrees that the Government should introduce automatic financial rights for cohabiting couples.


Supporters argue that the law needs to reflect the reality that millions of couples now live together without marrying. The Government says more than 3.5 million couples were cohabiting in 2025, compared with fewer than 1.5 million in 1996.


Critics, however, argue that some people deliberately choose not to marry because they want to keep their finances separate.


That creates an important question about personal choice: should couples who have consciously decided against marriage nevertheless acquire certain financial obligations simply because they have lived together for a specified period?


The consultation considered whether couples should be able to opt out of the proposed framework by mutual agreement.


## What should unmarried couples do now?


The proposed reforms are not currently law, so people should not assume that their former partner automatically has new rights over their assets.


However, the debate is a useful reminder for unmarried couples to understand how their finances are structured.


A **cohabitation agreement** can record how property, savings, debts and other financial responsibilities should be handled during the relationship and if the couple separates.


Property ownership is also important. If you jointly own a home, a **declaration of trust** can help establish how much of the property belongs to each person.


Wills are equally important.


Under current rules, an unmarried partner does not automatically inherit their partner's estate simply because they have lived together for many years. The Government is separately consulting on changes to inheritance rights for cohabitants where someone dies without a will.


For couples with significant assets, children, businesses or substantial pensions, professional legal and financial advice may therefore be worthwhile.


## The key takeaway


The proposed UK cohabitation law changes could give some unmarried partners greater financial protection when a relationship ends, particularly where one partner would otherwise be unable to meet basic housing and living needs.


However, the proposals do **not** mean that every ex-partner would automatically receive half of your house, savings or pension.


The Government's consultation has now closed, and any future legislation could change before it becomes law.


For now, the most sensible step for unmarried couples is to understand who owns what, consider whether a cohabitation agreement is appropriate, review property arrangements and make sure wills reflect their wishes.


As family structures continue to change, the legal rules governing relationships are likely to remain an important issue for household finances.

The proposed cohabitation reforms are not the same as current law and may change before any legislation is introduced or comes into force. Rules can also differ across the UK, so readers in England and Wales should seek advice from a suitably qualified professional about their individual circumstances.
